facts.statement: The only known species, Apsaravis ukhaana, lived approximately 78 million years ago during the Campanian age of the Late Cretaceous.
facts.quote: The single known species, Apsaravis ukhaana, lived about 78 million years ago, in the Campanian age of the Cretaceous period.

facts.statement: Fossils of Apsaravis were discovered in the Camel's Humps sublocality of the Djadokhta Formation at Ukhaa Tolgod in the Gobi Desert of Mongolia.
facts.quote: Its fossilized remains were found in the Camel's Humps sublocality of the Djadokhta Formation, at Ukhaa Tolgod in the Gobi Desert of Mongolia.

facts.statement: The genus Apsaravis was described by scientists Mark Norell and Jack Clarke in 2001.
facts.quote: It was described by Norell and Clarke (2001).

facts.statement: Researchers believe Apsaravis lived in a very arid, open landscape that was likely hotter than today with intermittent rainfall.
facts.quote: Its habitat was presumably very arid open landscape much like it is today, perhaps hotter still and with more (but nonetheless intermittent) rain.

facts.statement: Apsaravis possesses anatomical features found in both the primitive bird group Sauriurae and the lineage leading to modern birds, Ornithurae.
facts.quote: Apsaravis has features of both Sauriurae and Ornithurae.

facts.statement: Apsaravis displays advanced bird-like traits such as at least ten sacral vertebrae, a patellar groove on the femur, and an anterior sternal keel.
facts.quote: Apsaravis has several characters that place it near Aves (sensu Gauthier), including the presence of at least ten sacral vertebrae, a pubis and ischium that are closely appressed, distal pubes that do not touch, an 'obturator flange' on the ischium, loss of the cuppedicus muscle fossa on the ilium, a patellar groove on the distal femur, an anterior sternal keel, completely heterocoelus vertebrae, curved scapular shaft, and several features of the forelimb, ankle, and foot.

facts.statement: Despite its advanced features, Apsaravis retains primitive traits like a narrow intercondylar groove and barrel-shaped tibiotarsal condyles shared with early theropods.
facts.quote: Apsaravis also retains primitive characters shared with Enantiornithes and more basal theropods, including a narrow intercondylar groove and barrel-shaped condyles of the tibiotarsus, a dorsal fossa of the coracoid, into which the supracoracoideus nerve foramen opens, and several features of the humerus.

facts.statement: Apsaravis is the most primitive bird known to have an extensor process, a bony projection on the first finger bone that aids in automating wing extension during flight.
facts.quote: Apsaravis is the most basal bird that possesses an extensor process. This is a bony projection on metacarpal I that develops at the insertion of the m.extensor metacarpi radialis muscle and the propatagial ligaments.

facts.statement: Scientists debate whether the discovery of Apsaravis means the group Enantiornithes is paraphyletic, suggesting these birds were actually ancestors to modern birds rather than a separate side branch.
facts.quote: The discovery of further basal ornithurine fossils like Apsaravis could render the Enantiornithes paraphyletic.

facts.statement: Phylogenetic analysis places Apsaravis as the most basal member of the Ornithurae lineage, making it more advanced than Enantiornithes and Patagopteryx.
facts.quote: Clarke and Norell (2002) found that Apsaravis is the most basal ornithurine bird, but more advanced than Enantiornithes and Patagopteryx.

rejected.statement: Because Apsaravis was found in a sand dune environment and lacks aquatic adaptations, it proves that not all early modern birds were restricted to shorebird habitats.
rejected.quote: Apsaravis, however, was found in a sand dune environment, and it has no obviously aquatic anatomical adaptations, giving clear evidence that not all early members of Ornithurae were shorebirds.
